title: Theorists of War: Sun Tzu to Clausewitz
description: The two foundational frameworks for thinking about armed conflict

concepts.title: Sun Tzu and the Art of Indirect Approach
concepts.contentHtml:
The Art of War, attributed to Sun Tzu and likely compiled in China during the Warring States period (5th-3rd century BCE), is the oldest surviving treatise on strategy. Its core claim is that the supreme excellence of arms is to subdue the enemy without fighting. War is treated as a calculated extension of statecraft, weighed against five constant factors: moral influence, weather, terrain, command, and doctrine.

Sun Tzu emphasises deception ("all warfare is based on deception"), intelligence, and the manipulation of shi — strategic configuration or potential energy. Force should be applied where the enemy is unprepared and cannot respond. Direct (zheng) and indirect (qi) methods are paired: the orthodox fixes the enemy in place while the unorthodox delivers the decisive blow.

The text was rediscovered in the West in the 20th century and has shaped figures as different as Mao Zedong, Vo Nguyen Giap, and contemporary business strategists. Critics caution that its aphoristic style invites cherry-picking. Read carefully, it is not a manual for avoiding combat but for ensuring that when combat occurs, the outcome has already been decided by preparation, position, and information.

concepts.title: Clausewitz: War as the Continuation of Politics
concepts.contentHtml:
Carl von Clausewitz (1780-1831), a Prussian officer who served against Napoleon, wrote Vom Kriege (On War), published posthumously in 1832 by his widow. The book is unfinished, often opaque, and almost universally cited as the most important Western work on the subject.

Clausewitz's central proposition is that war is the continuation of politics by other means. War has no internal logic of its own; it is an instrument of policy, and its conduct must be subordinated to political ends. He distinguishes absolute war — an abstract ideal of unlimited violence — from real war, which is constrained by friction, exhaustion, terrain, and political restraint.

His enduring contributions include the concepts of fog of war (uncertainty about enemy and friendly positions), friction (the accumulation of small obstacles that derail plans), the culminating point of victory (where an offensive becomes vulnerable), and the centre of gravity (the source of an enemy's power). Clausewitz also rejected systematic doctrines that promised victory through fixed rules — a quiet rebuke to his contemporary Antoine-Henri Jomini.

concepts.title: The Trinity and the Limits of Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Late in On War, Clausewitz formulates his paradoxical trinity: war is governed by three forces — primordial violence, hatred, and enmity (the people); the play of chance and probability (the army and its commander); and reason, the subordination of war to policy (the government). A successful theory of war, he argues, must hold these three in dynamic balance rather than reduce one to the others.

The trinity has been used to explain why wars can escalate beyond political control (when popular passion overrides reason), why brilliant generalship can fail (when policy is incoherent), and why conventional militaries struggle against insurgencies (the people are mobilised against, not for, the state).

Clausewitz also stressed the limits of doctrine. Strategy is not a science of recipes but a domain of judgement under uncertainty. The competent commander internalises principles deeply enough to apply them flexibly. This is why his work resists translation into checklists. Modern critics — including Martin van Creveld and John Keegan — have argued that the trinitarian state-vs-state model fails to describe tribal, religious, or non-state violence, prompting ongoing debate over whether Clausewitz's framework is timeless or specifically European and post-Westphalian.

title: Pre-Modern Tactics: Phalanx to Pike-and-Shot
description: Two thousand years of formation, weapon, and counter-weapon

concepts.title: Phalanx, Legion, and the Cavalry Counter
concepts.contentHtml:
The Greek hoplite phalanx — densely packed citizens with overlapping shields and long thrusting spears — dominated Mediterranean infantry combat from roughly the 7th century BCE. Its strength was frontal cohesion; its weakness was rough terrain and exposed flanks. Philip II of Macedon and Alexander extended this with the longer sarissa pike and combined-arms wings of cavalry, decisively used at Gaugamela (331 BCE).

The Roman legion traded reach for flexibility. Maniples, and later cohorts, fought with the short gladius, javelin (pilum), and large rectangular shield. Rome's edge was less in any single weapon than in discipline, engineering, road-building, and logistics — including the capacity to rebuild armies after catastrophic defeats like Cannae (216 BCE), where Hannibal annihilated some 50,000-70,000 Romans through double envelopment.

Heavy cavalry repeatedly punished infantry that lacked combined arms. The Parthian cataphract humiliated Crassus at Carrhae (53 BCE). Centuries later, the Gothic horse broke a Roman army at Adrianople (378 CE), an event Edward Gibbon treated as a hinge in the decline of Rome and a harbinger of medieval cavalry's primacy.

concepts.title: The Longbow, the Crossbow, and Infantry's Return
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval European warfare is often caricatured as the era of the armoured knight. In practice, mounted men-at-arms were always supported by, and frequently defeated by, disciplined infantry with missile weapons. The English longbow, drawn from a deep yeoman recruitment base, devastated French chivalry at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), and Agincourt (1415). A trained archer could loose 10-12 arrows per minute at ranges past 200 metres.

The crossbow required less training but had a slower rate of fire and was famously condemned (against Christians) by the Second Lateran Council in 1139. Genoese crossbowmen and later mercenary companies kept it relevant for centuries. Both weapons reduced the social monopoly of the mounted noble: a commoner with a bow could kill a man worth a county's ransom.

The Swiss pike square revived dense infantry. Tightly drilled levies of free peasants armed with 5-6 metre pikes broke Burgundian cavalry at Grandson, Murten, and Nancy (1476-77), killing Charles the Bold and ending Burgundian independence. The Swiss model was widely imitated, especially by the German Landsknechte, and set the stage for the gunpowder transition.

concepts.title: Pike-and-Shot and the Gunpowder Transition
concepts.contentHtml:
From the late 15th century, the slow-firing arquebus and then the matchlock musket forced infantry to combine pikes (for protection against cavalry) with firearms (for ranged killing power). The resulting pike-and-shot formation defined European battles from the Italian Wars through the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648).

The Spanish tercio — a mixed block of pikemen and arquebusiers — dominated 16th-century battlefields, projecting power from Flanders to the New World. It was eventually outmanoeuvred by shallower, more mobile formations: the Dutch reforms of Maurice of Nassau, who reintroduced Roman-style drill and standardised volleys, and the Swedish reforms of Gustavus Adolphus, who lightened artillery and increased the proportion of musketeers, decisive at Breitenfeld (1631).

Historian Geoffrey Parker argues these changes amount to a military revolution: gunpowder-driven tactical change required larger, more disciplined, more expensive armies, which in turn drove the growth of the centralised fiscal-military state. Critics (Jeremy Black, Clifford Rogers) push back on the timing and uniqueness, but the broader claim — that war drove European state-building — remains influential.

title: Napoleonic Warfare and the Birth of Operational Art
description: Mass conscription, the corps system, and the campaign as the unit of strategy

concepts.title: Levée en Masse: The Nation in Arms
concepts.contentHtml:
The French Revolutionary decree of 23 August 1793 — the levée en masse — declared all unmarried men aged 18-25 permanently requisitioned for military service, with women, children, and the elderly assigned supporting roles. By 1794 France had mobilised some 800,000 soldiers, an unprecedented fraction of the population.

This was a political and social transformation as much as a military one. Earlier 18th-century armies were small, professional, and expensive; commanders avoided pitched battle to preserve them. The revolutionary citizen-soldier was cheap, replaceable, and ideologically motivated. France could absorb battles that would have destroyed the Bourbon army of Louis XVI.

Napoleon inherited and rationalised this system. By the 1812 invasion of Russia he commanded over 600,000 men of the Grande Armée, drawn from across the Empire. The political point — picked up later by Clausewitz — was that mass mobilisation pushed war closer to its absolute form. When the people are the army, the stakes are existential, restraint erodes, and conflicts that the cabinet wars of the Ancien Régime might have settled by limited campaigns become wars of national survival.

concepts.title: The Corps System and Operational Manoeuvre
concepts.contentHtml:
Napoleon's tactical reforms have been overstated; his operational reforms transformed warfare. He organised armies into self-contained corps d'armée, each combining infantry, cavalry, artillery, and staff capable of independent action for at least 24 hours. Corps marched on separate roads to ease supply and accelerate movement, then concentrated at the decisive point.

This dispersed-march, concentrated-fight pattern enabled the manoeuvre sur les derrières — appearing on the enemy's rear or flank with overwhelming force. Ulm (1805), where Napoleon enveloped an Austrian army of 60,000 with barely a battle, is the textbook case. Austerlitz (December 1805) is its pitched-battle counterpart: Napoleon abandoned the strong Pratzen Heights to lure the Austro-Russian army into attacking his right, then split their centre with a concealed reserve.

The corps system created a new layer of warfare between tactics (what happens in a battle) and strategy (what the war is for): the operational level, concerned with the design of campaigns. Soviet and German theorists in the 20th century would explicitly inherit this insight. The lineage from Napoleon's marshals through Helmuth von Moltke the Elder to modern joint doctrine runs through the corps and the staff system that managed it.

concepts.title: Jomini and the Geometric Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
Antoine-Henri Jomini (1779-1869), a Swiss-French officer who served Napoleon and later the Tsar, was the most widely read military theorist of the 19th century. His Précis de l'art de la guerre (1838) systematised Napoleonic practice into principles: concentrate force at the decisive point, operate on interior lines, attack the enemy's communications.

Where Clausewitz emphasised friction, contingency, and the political nature of war, Jomini emphasised geometry, lines of operation, and prescriptive maxims. His work was used at West Point through the American Civil War and shaped commanders on both sides — Henry Halleck translated Jomini, and Robert E. Lee's interior-lines defence reads as a Jominian textbook.

The Jomini-Clausewitz contrast remains the central methodological tension in military thought. Jomini gives officers usable rules; Clausewitz warns that any rule can be overturned by friction or politics. Modern doctrine tries to combine both: lists of principles of war (mass, manoeuvre, surprise, security, simplicity) acknowledge a Jominian inheritance, while insistence on commander's intent, mission command, and political subordination is recognisably Clausewitzian. Neither tradition has won; each guards against the other's failure mode.

title: Industrial Warfare and the Attritional Deadlock
description: Railroads, breech-loaders, machine guns, and the road to the Western Front

concepts.title: Railroads, Telegraphs, and the American Civil War
concepts.contentHtml:
The American Civil War (1861-1865) was the first conflict in which industrial logistics dominated outcomes. The Union's railroad network was roughly twice the Confederacy's, and Northern industry produced firearms, munitions, and rolling stock at scales the South could not match. Telegraph lines let Lincoln and Stanton manage theatres in near-real-time, an unprecedented compression of strategic decision cycles.

Tactically, the rifled musket — accurate to several hundred metres versus the smoothbore's 50-100 — made Napoleonic shoulder-to-shoulder assaults catastrophic. Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg (July 1863) lost over half its men in less than an hour. Defenders began entrenching routinely; the Petersburg siege (1864-65) prefigured the Western Front in its trench lines, mortars, and underground mining.

Grant's 1864-65 campaigns introduced the modern logic of attrition and economic warfare: pin Lee's army through continuous contact, while Sherman's march through Georgia and the Carolinas destroyed the South's ability to feed and supply itself. European observers — including Helmuth von Moltke, who reportedly called it "two armed mobs chasing each other around the country" — were slower to absorb its lessons than they should have been.

concepts.title: Breech-Loaders, Machine Guns, and Quick-Firing Artillery
concepts.contentHtml:
Between 1860 and 1914 the lethality of infantry fire grew by orders of magnitude. The bolt-action breech-loader (Dreyse, Chassepot, Mauser) raised practical rates of fire from 2-3 rounds per minute to 10-15 and let soldiers reload while prone. The Maxim machine gun (1884), the first true automatic, fired 600 rounds per minute from a single tripod-mounted weapon — equivalent to 80-100 rifles. Quick-firing artillery with hydraulic recoil (the French 75mm of 1897 was the prototype) could deliver 20+ rounds per minute without re-laying.

Smokeless powder, introduced in the late 1880s, removed the battlefield's white fog and made hidden positions far deadlier. The cumulative effect — predicted by the Polish banker Jan Bloch in his 1898 Future War, ridiculed at the time — was that any frontal assault against entrenched troops with modern weapons would fail with horrendous casualties.

Most general staffs absorbed this lesson incompletely. The Boer War (1899-1902) and Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) provided clear warnings: defensive firepower had outpaced infantry mobility. Yet 1914 plans on all sides still assumed short, mobile, decisive campaigns — the so-called cult of the offensive.

concepts.title: The Western Front and the Search for a Way Out
concepts.contentHtml:
By late 1914 the trenches stretched from the North Sea to Switzerland and the war on the Western Front became a problem of breaking through prepared defences faster than the defender could rail in reserves. Successive offensives — the Somme (1916), Verdun (1916), Passchendaele (1917) — produced casualty totals in the hundreds of thousands for territorial gains measured in kilometres.

Both sides searched for a tactical solution. The British developed creeping artillery barrages, sound-ranging for counter-battery fire, and the tank (Cambrai 1917). The Germans evolved infiltration tactics under Oskar von Hutier and Willy Rohr: small Stosstrupp squads bypassed strongpoints to attack rear command and artillery, breaking the linear defence pattern. The German Spring Offensives of 1918 used these methods to advance further than any front-line move since 1914 — but ran out of supply, manpower, and political will.

Historians now describe the gradual emergence of combined-arms tactics — coordinated infantry, artillery, armour, aviation — as the genuine "learning curve" of 1916-1918, even as the strategic deadlock dragged on. The lessons would shape interwar doctrine in Britain (Fuller, Liddell Hart), Germany (Guderian), and the Soviet Union (Tukhachevsky).

title: Combined Arms in WWII: Blitzkrieg, Deep Battle, Carriers
description: How three powers solved the breakthrough problem in three different ways

concepts.title: Blitzkrieg: Doctrine or Improvisation?
concepts.contentHtml:
The German campaigns of 1939-41 — Poland, France, the Balkans, the opening of Barbarossa — appeared to demonstrate a revolutionary new doctrine: Blitzkrieg, the coordinated use of armoured spearheads, motorised infantry, and tactical airpower (Stukas, mobile flak) to penetrate, encircle, and destroy enemy forces before they could reorganise. The fall of France in six weeks (May-June 1940) shocked observers who had expected another Western Front grind.

Recent historiography (Karl-Heinz Frieser, Blitzkrieg-Legende, 1995) argues the term itself was largely a postwar journalistic gloss. The Wehrmacht had no formal Blitzkrieg doctrine; what worked in 1940 was a combination of Bewegungskrieg (the older Prussian tradition of war of movement), Heinz Guderian's tactical insight that Panzers should mass rather than disperse, and substantial luck — the French were caught operationally rather than tactically defeated.

The German way of war retained a structural weakness: it could win opening campaigns spectacularly but lacked the strategic depth, logistics, and economic base for prolonged industrial warfare. Once the USSR and US mobilised, Germany faced exactly the attritional contest its doctrine could not win. Blitzkrieg was a tactical-operational style, not a strategy.

concepts.title: Soviet Deep Battle and Operational Manoeuvre
concepts.contentHtml:
While the Germans were solving the breakthrough problem at the tactical level, Soviet theorists in the 1920s and 30s — Mikhail Tukhachevsky, Vladimir Triandafillov, Georgii Isserson — developed deep battle (glubokii boi) and its operational extension, deep operations. The idea: simultaneously suppress the enemy's entire defensive depth with artillery, airpower, and successive echelons of mechanised forces, then exploit far into the rear to dislocate command and reserves.

Stalin's purges of 1937-38 destroyed the Red Army's senior leadership and set the doctrine back for years; the early disasters of 1941 partly reflect this. By 1943-45, however, the Red Army had reconstructed and applied deep operations on a continental scale. Operation Bagration (June-August 1944) destroyed Germany's Army Group Centre — over 25 divisions, perhaps 350,000-400,000 casualties — in a multi-front offensive that advanced 600 kilometres in two months.

Deep battle is the direct ancestor of NATO's later AirLand Battle doctrine and US Army FM 100-5 (1982 revision), which explicitly studied Soviet operational thought. The lineage is one of the more striking examples of intellectual transmission between rival military traditions.

concepts.title: Carriers, Strategic Bombing, and the Pacific
concepts.contentHtml:
The interwar US and Imperial Japanese navies both correctly identified the aircraft carrier as the new capital ship, displacing the battleship that had dominated since Trafalgar. The Pacific War's decisive engagements — Coral Sea (May 1942) and especially Midway (June 1942), where US carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers in a single day — were fought between forces that never sighted each other on the surface.

Strategic bombing, by contrast, repeatedly underdelivered on its prewar promises. Giulio Douhet had argued in The Command of the Air (1921) that bomber fleets could break civilian morale and end wars without ground campaigns. The reality of the British and US bomber offensives over Germany was high crew loss rates, German war production that actually peaked in 1944 under bombing, and contested moral and military verdicts on city attacks like Hamburg, Dresden, and Tokyo.

The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945) were technically the strategic-bombing thesis vindicated; debates continue over whether they were militarily decisive in Japan's surrender or whether Soviet entry into the war was equally or more important. Either way, they ended one era of war and opened another.

title: Nuclear Strategy and Deterrence Theory
description: Schelling, MAD, and the strange logic of weapons not used

concepts.title: Deterrence and the Schelling Framework
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear weapons changed strategy by making decisive military victory between great powers potentially suicidal. The central problem became deterrence: persuading an opponent that the cost of attacking will exceed any conceivable gain. Thomas Schelling, in The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966), supplied much of the conceptual vocabulary still in use.

Schelling distinguished deterrence (preventing an action) from compellence (forcing an action), and emphasised the role of credibility, commitment, and signalling. A threat is only effective if the adversary believes you will carry it out — which often means tying your own hands. He famously analysed the manipulation of risk, the "threat that leaves something to chance," and the bargaining structure of crisis behaviour.

Game theory underpins much of this: nuclear stand-offs resemble games of chicken and prisoner's dilemma, where rational players can reach disastrous outcomes. Schelling's contribution was to show that strategy could be analysed as the interdependent decision-making of opponents, not merely as the application of force. He won the 2005 Nobel in economics partly for this work.

concepts.title: MAD, Counterforce, and Targeting Doctrine
concepts.contentHtml:
Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD) describes a strategic situation in which both sides have second-strike capability — enough surviving weapons after absorbing a first strike to destroy the attacker. Under MAD, neither side has a rational incentive to start a nuclear war, since doing so guarantees its own destruction. The condition emerged in roughly the late 1960s with the deployment of SSBNs (ballistic missile submarines), which are nearly impossible to find and pre-emptively destroy.

Strategists distinguish countervalue targeting (cities, population, industry — the classic deterrent threat) from counterforce targeting (the enemy's nuclear forces and command). Counterforce sounds more humane but is destabilising: weapons accurate enough to destroy hardened silos invite a first-strike race, since whoever launches first might disarm the other. The MIRV (multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle), introduced in the 1970s, made counterforce more feasible and triggered the SALT/START arms control efforts.

The 1972 ABM Treaty restricted missile defences precisely because effective defence would undermine MAD. The argument — counterintuitive but logically tight — was that vulnerability stabilises deterrence. Withdrawal from the ABM Treaty in 2002 reopened debates about strategic stability that remain active in the era of hypersonic glide vehicles and renewed great-power competition.

concepts.title: Escalation, Limited War, and Nuclear Taboos
concepts.contentHtml:
If unrestrained nuclear war is suicidal, can limited nuclear war be fought? Theorists from Henry Kissinger (Nuclear Weapons and Foreign Policy, 1957) to Herman Kahn (On Thermonuclear War, 1960; On Escalation, 1965) tried to answer yes, mapping out ladders of escalation with dozens of rungs from sub-conventional crisis through tactical nuclear use to spasmodic civilian extermination.

Kahn was widely caricatured (he was a model for Dr. Strangelove) but his analytical point was serious: deterrence requires credible options at every level. If the only response to a Soviet move into West Germany is all-out nuclear war, the threat is not credible and deterrence fails. NATO's flexible response doctrine (1967) and tactical nuclear weapons in Europe were attempts to fill the gap.

Critics — including Robert Jervis and Bernard Brodie — questioned whether escalation could really be controlled once nuclear weapons were used. The empirical record is the nuclear taboo: no nuclear weapon has been used in conflict since 1945, despite multiple wars involving nuclear powers. Whether this reflects deliberate restraint, deterrence working, or simple luck remains contested. The 2022 Russian threats over Ukraine reopened the question for the first time in a generation.

concepts.title: Mao and the Theory of People's War
concepts.contentHtml:
Mao Zedong's writings on guerrilla warfare — especially On Guerrilla Warfare (1937) and On Protracted War (1938) — synthesised a generation of Chinese revolutionary practice into the most influential 20th-century theory of insurgency. Mao's three-phase model: strategic defensive (organisation, propaganda, hit-and-run), strategic stalemate (expanded guerrilla bases, mobile warfare), and strategic offensive (conventional operations to seize cities and state power).

The political dimension is primary. The famous metaphor — "the guerrilla must move amongst the people as a fish swims in the sea" — places population control and political mobilisation above pure military action. Without the population, the insurgent has no intelligence, supplies, or recruits; with it, the insurgent is invisible.

Mao's framework shaped Vo Nguyen Giap in Vietnam, who applied it against France (climaxing at Dien Bien Phu, 1954) and the United States. It also influenced Latin American revolutionaries (with Che Guevara's foco theory as a contested variant), the Algerian FLN, and parts of the Cuban revolution. Critics note that Mao's success depended on specific conditions — Japanese invasion, weak Nationalist control, vast rural depth — that don't generalise everywhere.

concepts.title: Galula and Classical Counterinsurgency
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential Western response to Mao came from David Galula, a French officer who served in Algeria. His Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice (1964) argued that COIN is fundamentally political, not military: the contest is over which side can credibly govern and protect a population, with combat operations as a supporting activity.

Galula's prescriptions: separate the insurgent from the population, then provide security, basic services, and political incorporation; use minimum force consistent with that goal; accept that the campaign will be slow and that 80% of the effort will be non-kinetic. He stressed that the counterinsurgent has the harder job — the insurgent need only spread chaos, while the state must maintain functioning order.

The French in Algeria (1954-62) won most tactical engagements, including the brutal Battle of Algiers (1957), but lost strategically — the use of torture and collective punishment alienated Algerian and metropolitan French opinion alike. The lesson, learned painfully, was that tactical methods that contradict the political objective destroy it. Galula's work was rediscovered by US officers (notably David Petraeus) in the mid-2000s and informed FM 3-24 (2006), the COIN field manual that shaped the Iraq surge.

concepts.title: Vietnam, Afghanistan, and the Limits of Outside Intervention
concepts.contentHtml:
The Vietnam War (US involvement c. 1965-73) became the defining failure of conventional firepower against political insurgency. The Tet Offensive (January-February 1968) was a tactical defeat for the Viet Cong — they suffered enormous casualties and failed to spark a general uprising — but a strategic victory: the visible breadth of the attacks contradicted official US claims of progress and shattered domestic political support for the war.

The Soviet war in Afghanistan (1979-89) and the US war in Afghanistan (2001-21) both ended with the foreign intervener withdrawing while the insurgents (Mujahideen, then Taliban) eventually took or retook the country. Both campaigns featured competent tactical performance, advanced technology, and substantial reconstruction spending — and both foundered on the inability to build a legitimate, durable local state.

The structural lesson, repeatedly drawn and repeatedly forgotten: outside powers can usually destroy regimes but cannot reliably build them. Insurgencies that retain external sanctuary, ideological coherence, and a credible claim to represent the nation typically outlast foreign occupations. The 21st-century policy question — when, if ever, large-scale COIN is worth the cost — remains contested, with most Western militaries pivoting back toward great-power competition since the late 2010s.

title: RMA and 21st-Century Warfare
description: Precision, networks, drones, cyber, and Ukraine 2022

concepts.title: The Revolution in Military Affairs
concepts.contentHtml:
The Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA) thesis — developed in the late Soviet General Staff under Marshal Ogarkov in the 1980s, then adopted enthusiastically in the US — held that information technology, precision-guided munitions (PGMs), and networked sensors would transform warfare as profoundly as gunpowder or industrialisation. Desert Storm (1991) was the first large showcase: a US-led coalition destroyed an Iraqi army of nominally similar size in 100 hours of ground combat at extremely lopsided casualty ratios.

Key RMA components: stealth (F-117, B-2), PGMs (laser- and GPS-guided bombs, Tomahawk cruise missiles), C4ISR (command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) integrating sensors and shooters in near-real-time, and satellite-enabled navigation and targeting. Targets that once took dozens of unguided bombs to destroy could be killed with a single weapon.

John Boyd's OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) — developed from his Korean War fighter pilot experience — became the conceptual shorthand for RMA-era operational thinking: get inside the enemy's decision cycle, force them to react to outdated information. Critics, especially after Iraq 2003-11, argued the RMA over-promised against state opponents and failed entirely against insurgencies, where networking sensors does not solve the political problem.

concepts.title: Drones, Cyber, and the New Tools
concepts.contentHtml:
Three technologies define early-21st-century warfare. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) evolved from reconnaissance platforms (Predator, 1995) to armed strike systems (the first Hellfire-equipped Predator killed an al-Qaeda target in Yemen in 2002) to disposable munitions like the Iranian Shahed-136 and Ukrainian-modified DJI commercial quadcopters. The cost asymmetry is striking: a US$500 quadcopter can disable a multi-million-dollar tank if used skilfully.

Cyber operations emerged as a domain of conflict between peace and war. Stuxnet (discovered 2010), a US-Israeli operation that destroyed Iranian uranium centrifuges, demonstrated that code could deliver kinetic effects without troops. Russian operations against Ukrainian power grids (2015, 2016) and the Sandworm and APT28 groups extended the pattern. Cyber's distinctive features: ambiguous attribution, uncertain damage assessment, and a low threshold for use compared to kinetic alternatives.

Hybrid warfare, sometimes labelled the "Gerasimov doctrine" (a misreading of a 2013 article by Russian Chief of Staff Valery Gerasimov), describes the integration of conventional, irregular, cyber, information, and economic instruments below the threshold of overt war. Whether this is genuinely new or simply the old practice of subversion with better tools is contested in the literature.

concepts.title: Ukraine 2022 and What It Has Taught
concepts.contentHtml:
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine (February 2022) became the first large-scale war between roughly conventional militaries in Europe since 1945, and a live laboratory for 21st-century concepts. Several early assumptions were upended.

First, the tank is not dead, but it must be combined-arms protected. Without infantry screens, drone overwatch, and electronic warfare, armour is highly vulnerable to top-attack munitions (Javelin, NLAW, FPV drones). Second, the war restored the importance of artillery and ammunition production at scales unseen since Korea — both sides have at times fired 10,000+ shells per day, exhausting Western stockpiles and exposing thinned defence-industrial bases. Third, commercial technology (Starlink, off-the-shelf drones, smartphone-based artillery correction apps like GIS Arta) has been militarily decisive in ways prewar doctrine did not anticipate.

Fourth, and most uncomfortably for RMA optimism, the war has settled into positional, attritional patterns reminiscent of 1916-1918 — extensive trench networks, contested airspace, and slow advances measured in kilometres per month. Pervasive ISR makes large mechanised manoeuvre nearly impossible; the side that masses is the side that gets struck. The implications for force structure, industrial policy, and doctrine are still being absorbed by NATO members and by potential adversaries watching closely.

title: Logistics, Geography, and the Economics of War
description: Mahan, Mackinder, van Creveld, and Lanchester's quiet equations

concepts.title: Sea Power, Land Power, and Geopolitics
concepts.contentHtml:
Alfred Thayer Mahan, a US naval officer, published The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660-1783 in 1890. His argument: control of the seas — secured by concentrated battle fleets, overseas bases, and a strong merchant marine — is the decisive factor in great-power competition. Mahan's work directly shaped the Anglo-German naval race before WWI, the build-up of the US Navy under Theodore Roosevelt, and Imperial Japanese strategy.

The land-power counter came from the British geographer Halford Mackinder. His 1904 paper The Geographical Pivot of History introduced the concept of the Heartland — the great Eurasian interior, inaccessible to sea power. "Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the World." Mackinder's framework became foundational to 20th-century geopolitics, including German Geopolitik (Karl Haushofer) and US Cold War containment thinking through Nicholas Spykman's modification (the Rimland).

Both theorists exemplify strategic geography: the claim that physical position and resource access constrain even the cleverest strategy. Modern equivalents include analyses of chokepoints (Hormuz, Malacca, Suez), undersea cable routes, and rare-earth supply chains. Geography is rarely destiny, but it is rarely irrelevant.

concepts.title: Logistics: The Iron Constraint
concepts.contentHtml:
An aphorism widely attributed to Omar Bradley summarises the field: amateurs talk tactics; professionals study logistics. Martin van Creveld's Supplying War (1977) is the standard scholarly treatment, tracing how logistical capacity has set the outer envelope of military possibility from the early modern period to the 20th century.

Van Creveld shows that pre-rail armies were limited to roughly the distance their wagons could travel before consuming their own load — a few hundred kilometres at most without local foraging. Napoleonic armies stretched this with requisition (living off occupied territory), which worked in agricultural Central Europe but failed in the burned-over Russia of 1812. The railroad freed armies from animal-drawn supply but tied them to fixed lines — explaining the operational geography of WWI and many WWII campaigns.

Modern logistics is even more demanding. A US armoured division consumes hundreds of tons of fuel per day; a carrier strike group requires near-continuous replenishment. The 1991 Gulf War involved moving roughly 500,000 troops and millions of tons of materiel halfway around the world — an industrial-scale operation that took six months. Logistics constrains strategy more often than strategy constrains logistics, and a campaign plan that ignores supply lines tends to fail at exactly the moment it appears to be succeeding.

concepts.title: Lanchester's Equations and the Mathematics of Attrition
concepts.contentHtml:
The British engineer Frederick Lanchester published a set of differential equations in 1916 modelling combat attrition. The Lanchester linear law applies to ancient hand-to-hand combat: losses are roughly proportional to force size, and a 2:1 advantage gives a 2:1 outcome. The Lanchester square law applies to aimed ranged combat: combat power scales with the square of force size, so a 2:1 numerical advantage produces a 4:1 effective advantage.

The square law explains why concentration of force is so important in modern firepower-dominated combat, and why an attacker that can defeat enemy detachments in detail before they unite has a disproportionate edge. It also formalises Nelson's instinct at Trafalgar (1805): break the enemy line, fight superior locally, win even when outnumbered overall.

Real combat is much messier than Lanchester models — terrain, morale, command, surprise, logistics, and combined arms all introduce nonlinearities the equations ignore. Modern operational research uses Lanchester as a baseline against which to measure departures from pure attrition. The deeper lesson is that quantitative analysis has its place in strategy, but always sits on top of the political, human, and contingent factors that Clausewitz refused to let his readers forget.
